meta.source_text: Rahlfs-Hanhart, Septuaginta (composite of A-text [Alexandrinus] and B-text [Vaticanus])
meta.translators: Alexandrian Jewish translators (3rd–2nd c. BCE), with later revision
meta.date: 3rd–2nd century BCE (A-text shows later stylistic revision)

preamble.summary: Judges is preserved in the Greek tradition in two distinct recensions — the A-text (represented chiefly by Alexandrinus) and the B-text (chiefly Vaticanus) — that differ substantially from each other and from MT. Rahlfs prints them in parallel. The A-text is longer and often reflects a later stylistic revision closer to Theodotion; the B-text is often judged closer to the original Old Greek. Where this file cites a 'LXX reading,' it is the B-text unless otherwise noted.
preamble.notable_variants: The Song of Deborah (Judges 5) is one of the most textually complex poems in the Hebrew Bible, and the two Greek recensions diverge sharply from each other and from MT. The Samson cycle (13–16) carries several LXX pluses, particularly around the Nazirite vow. The judges-refrain formulas use LXX vocabulary that shaped NT rhetoric about the monarchy.
preamble.theological_legacy: LXX Judges gave early Christian writers the Nazirite vocabulary (naziraion theou) that frames John the Baptist narratives, the 'Spirit rushing upon' formula for charismatic anointing, and the refrain of 'no king in Israel / everyone did what was right in his own eyes' that Acts and Paul invoke when describing leaderless or law-less humanity. The two-recension transmission of Judges is itself a reminder that the 'Septuagint' is a family of Greek Bibles, not a single text.

renderings.lxx_reading: ἐν τῷ ἄρξασθαι ἀρχηγοὺς ἐν Ισραηλ (B-text) / ἀπεκαλύφθη ἀποκάλυμμα ἐν Ισραηλ (A-text)
renderings.lxx_rendering: When leaders began to lead in Israel (B) / An uncovering was uncovered in Israel (A)
notes: The opening of the Song of Deborah is one of the most linguistically contested verses in the Hebrew Bible. The verb para can mean 'to let loose,' 'to uncover,' 'to lead,' or even 'to have long hair' (as in Nazirite consecration). The two Greek recensions split cleanly: B reads 'leaders leading,' A reads 'uncovering uncovered.'

The archēgos vocabulary of B-text Judges is the same word Hebrews 2:10 and Hebrews 12:2 use of Christ — 'the archēgos of their salvation,' 'the archēgos and perfecter of faith.' The LXX-Judges military-leader sense carries directly into Hebrews' pioneer-and-trailblazer Christology.

renderings.lxx_reading: οἱ ἀγαπῶντες αὐτὸν ὡς ἔξοδος ἡλίου ἐν δυνάμει αὐτοῦ
renderings.mt_rendering: may those who love Him be like the sun rising in its full strength
renderings.lxx_rendering: those who love him as the going-out of the sun in its power
notes: The LXX's exodos hēliou ('going-out of the sun') uses the same noun — exodos — that Luke 9:31 uses for Jesus' death and resurrection in the Transfiguration scene: 'they were speaking of his exodos which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem.'

The sun-rising-in-strength image attached to those who love God also shapes Matthew 13:43 — 'then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father' — where the LXX vocabulary underlies the eschatological glorification imagery.

renderings.lxx_reading: ὅτι ναζιραῖον θεοῦ ἔσται τὸ παιδάριον
renderings.mt_rendering: the boy will be a Nazirite dedicated to God
renderings.lxx_rendering: for the child shall be a Nazirite of God
notes: The LXX transliterates Hebrew nazir as naziraios — giving Greek and subsequent Western languages the word 'Nazirite.' The translators chose transliteration over translation (e.g., they did not render it as hagios, 'holy one,' though the sense is close).

Luke 1:15 — on John the Baptist — echoes this LXX Nazirite formula: 'he will be great before the Lord, and he shall drink no wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb.' The three Nazirite elements (abstention from wine, uncut hair, lifelong consecration from the womb) line up with Samson and Samuel.

Jesus is also called 'Nazōraios' (Matt 2:23, etc.) — a word that plays on Nazareth and, in the text of Matthew 2:23 ('he shall be called a Nazōraios'), may also fuse Isaiah 11:1 netser with the nazir/naziraios tradition of Judges 13 and Numbers 6.

renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ κατηύθυνεν ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν πνεῦμα κυρίου
renderings.mt_rendering: The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him
renderings.lxx_rendering: And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him
notes: The LXX renders Hebrew tsalach ('rushed, seized, came upon mightily') with various Greek verbs across Judges — katheuthynen here (14:6), hēlato ('leaped upon,' 14:19, 15:14), and others. The net effect is a cluster of Greek verbs describing the Spirit's sudden empowering descent.

Luke uses the same Pneuma kyriou formula at Acts 1:8, 10:38, and throughout the early Christian narrative. The charismatic-anointing sense of LXX Judges — the Spirit rushing on a leader to equip them for a specific deliverance — shapes Luke-Acts' language for the Spirit's descent on believers.

renderings.lxx_reading: ἅγιος θεοῦ ἐγώ εἰμι ἐκ κοιλίας μητρός μου (B-text) / ναζιραῖος θεοῦ ἐγώ εἰμι (A-text)
renderings.mt_rendering: I have been a Nazirite of God from my mother's womb
renderings.lxx_rendering: I am a holy one of God from my mother's womb (B) / I am a Nazirite of God (A)
notes: The B-text renders nazir as hagios ('holy one'); the A-text keeps naziraios. The two Greek recensions witness to two distinct solutions for bringing a Hebrew cultic status-term into Greek.

The B-text's hagios theou is the very title used of Jesus by the demoniacs in Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34: 'I know who you are — the Holy One of God' (ho hagios tou theou). Some scholars have suggested the demoniacs' recognition of Jesus as 'the Holy One of God' may invoke the Samson-Nazirite category in its LXX B-text form — a strong-man-of-God figure empowered by the Spirit.

renderings.mt_reading: זָכְרֵנִי נָא וְחַזְּקֵנִי נָא אַךְ הַפַּעַם הַזֶּה
renderings.lxx_reading: μνήσθητί μου καὶ ἐνίσχυσόν με δὴ πλὴν ἔτι τὸ ἅπαξ τοῦτο
renderings.mt_rendering: Lord GOD, remember me! Strengthen me just this one time
renderings.lxx_rendering: remember me and strengthen me this once more
notes: The LXX's mnēsthēti mou ('remember me') is the same verb in the same mood that the thief on the cross uses at Luke 23:42: mnēsthēti mou, kyrie, hotan elthēs eis tēn basileian sou ('remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom').

The verbal parallel is striking: both are last-words petitions, both invoke divine memory as the ground of rescue, both come from figures on the edge of death. Luke's careful composition is likely aware of the LXX Judges resonance.

renderings.mt_reading: בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
renderings.lxx_reading: ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις οὐκ ἦν βασιλεὺς ἐν Ισραηλ ἀνὴρ τὸ εὐθὲς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ ἐποίει
renderings.mt_rendering: In those days, there was no king in Israel. Everyone did whatever seemed right in their own eyes.
renderings.lxx_rendering: In those days there was no king in Israel; each man did what was right in his own eyes
notes: The refrain of Judges (17:6, 18:1, 19:1, 21:25) circulates in its LXX form in early Jewish and Christian political rhetoric as a description of anarchy. The LXX's to euthes en ophthalmois autou ('the right in his own eyes') is a fixed collocation that reappears in Psalm LXX forms.

Paul's charge in Romans 3:11 — 'no one understands' — and Romans 14:5's milder 'each person must be fully convinced in his own mind' both sit inside the same semantic field as the LXX refrain: the question of moral authority when there is no shared standard.

renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ηὐξήθη τὸ παιδάριον καὶ εὐλόγησεν αὐτὸ κύριος
renderings.mt_rendering: The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him
renderings.lxx_rendering: And the child grew, and the Lord blessed him
notes: Luke 1:80 and Luke 2:40 both use this LXX growth-and-blessing formula: 'the child grew and became strong in spirit' (John the Baptist); 'the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom; and the favor of God was upon him' (Jesus). The birth-narrative template for both Gospel infancies traces through LXX Judges 13:24 (Samson) and 1 Samuel 2:26 (Samuel).
Luke's deliberate echo of the LXX Samson/Samuel formula places Jesus and John in the lineage of promised-birth deliverers commissioned from the womb.
